source: Hersche et al. (2024/25) Towards Learning to Reason: Comparing LLMs with Neuro-Symbolic on Arithmetic Relations in Abstract Reasoning
finding: The paper tests two ways to run an LLM on I-RAVEN. Discriminative: show the answer candidates and ask which fits. Predictive: show only the context matrix, ask the model to write the missing panel's attribute values, then CODE picks the candidate with the most overlap. The authors say predictive makes the LLM work as humans do: build a solution first, then pick the closest option. This is the clearest LLM test of constructive matching versus option-based choice.
numbers: Center constellation of I-RAVEN, Table III, no extra tricks. Discriminative: GPT-4 56.0 to 60.0 percent, Llama-3 70B 22.4 to 22.8 percent. Predictive: GPT-4 74.8, Llama-3 70B 79.0. Predictive plus per-attribute queries: 91.4 (GPT-4), 83.2 (Llama-3). Plus self-consistency n=7: GPT-4 93.2, Llama-3 84.8.
quote: the predictive classification can be seen as a more guided approach that helps LLM to solve the task
limits: Symbolic attribute descriptions, not pixels (oracle perception). Center constellation only. Exact row-to-setting mapping of the first two discriminative rows is garbled in the PDF text. Older models (GPT-4-0613, Llama-3 70B).
agent_relevance: Strong support for S3 then S4: have the model build an answer from the examples alone, and let code do the matching against candidates. Keeps the model out of option-by-option elimination.

source: Hersche et al. (2024/25) Towards Learning to Reason (same paper), arithmetic rule weakness
finding: Constructive prediction works for easy rules but not for arithmetic rules. Splitting the problem into one query per attribute lifts arithmetic-rule accuracy a lot for GPT-4 but not enough for Llama-3.
numbers: Table IV, attribute-value accuracy with self-consistency n=7. GPT-4 arithmetic rule: 27.1 percent in one entangled query, 73.6 percent with disentangled queries. Llama-3 70B: 31.0 vs 45.0. Constant, progression, distribute-three rules are at 91.6 to 100 percent for both.
limits: Same setup as c01. Disentangling costs 3x the queries.
agent_relevance: The build step fails on rules that need computation. Offload arithmetic to code or split by attribute; do not just ask for a longer chain of thought.

source: Hersche et al. (2024/25) Towards Learning to Reason, I-RAVEN-X generalisation
finding: A neuro-symbolic system that abduces rules and builds the answer (ARLC) holds up when the matrix gets longer and value ranges bigger. LLM arithmetic accuracy collapses to near zero.
numbers: LLM arithmetic-rule accuracy drops to sub-10 percent as the dynamic range goes from 10 up to 1000 (c05 table: GPT-4 arithmetic 73.6 to 8.4 percent with ICL prompts). ARLC accuracy stays high (98.4 percent reported in the abstract region).
limits: Abstract text gives the headline; table detail in c05.
agent_relevance: For long or large-valued matrices, an exact program (a constructed solver) beats text reasoning. This is an argument for code-side construction in S3.

source: Camposampiero et al. (2025) Can Large Reasoning Models do Analogical Reasoning under Perceptual Uncertainty?
finding: Reasoning models (o3-mini, DeepSeek R1) do much better than GPT-4 on I-RAVEN with far fewer prompts, but fall to near chance when confounding attributes and smoothed value distributions simulate imperfect perception. More reasoning tokens did not help.
numbers: o3-mini: 86.6 percent on I-RAVEN to 17.0 percent on I-RAVEN-X with uncertainty, with 3.4x more reasoning tokens. R1: 80.6 to 23.2 percent. Neuro-symbolic ARLC: 98.6 to 88.0 percent.
limits: Symbolic input, discriminative format. Only two reasoning models.
agent_relevance: When the evidence is noisy or has distractor features, longer thinking does not rescue the answer. Cut noise at S1/S2 (input hygiene) rather than think longer.

source: Camposampiero et al. (2025), Table 1 on I-RAVEN and I-RAVEN-X
finding: Direct side-by-side of LLMs and reasoning models, with full-task and arithmetic-rule accuracy and token counts. Reasoning models spend about two orders of magnitude more output tokens than LLMs.
numbers: I-RAVEN 3x3 task accuracy: Llama-3 70B 85.0; GPT-4 93.2 (21 prompts, ICL) ; o3-mini medium 86.6 with 5445 tokens; o3-mini high 92.6 with 9867 tokens; R1 80.6 with 4486 tokens. Arithmetic accuracy: GPT-4 73.6, o3-mini 74.4 to 86.1. I-RAVEN-X range 1000: GPT-4 arithmetic 8.4 or 0.4 depending on setup, o3-mini 60.8, R1 65.8.
limits: GPT-4 and Llama numbers are copied from Hersche et al.; prompt budgets differ (21 or 7 prompts vs 1).
agent_relevance: Test-time reasoning buys robustness on rule application but costs 100x tokens. Spend by difficulty (G12).

source: Camposampiero et al. (2025), generative vs discriminative design choice
finding: The authors switched from predicting the missing panel to choosing among candidates because, when free to build an answer, reasoning models sometimes found valid-looking but irrelevant relations in the data (e.g. between binary encodings of values). The candidate list quietly restricts the model to the rule family the test uses.
numbers: Observed qualitatively in early evaluation; no accuracy given for this switch.
quote: the discriminative approach implicitly biases the model into evaluating only the rules defined in RPM
limits: Anecdotal. Opposite direction from c01: there, predictive helped with plain LLMs.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition on building first: an unconstrained construction can invent a rule that fits the examples but is not the intended one. Keep the candidate set as a sanity check (S4/S7), do not drop it.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) How Far Are We from Intelligent Visual Deductive Reasoning?
finding: Vision-language models are near chance on image RPMs (Mensa, IntelligenceTest, RAVEN). Models rank in the 2 to 8 percentile on the Mensa test. They never voice doubt even when they are guessing.
numbers: Table 2 (10 repeats), GPT-4V 0-shot accuracy: Mensa 24 percent, IntelligenceTest 16, RAVEN 12 (random: 16, 16, 12). Gemini Pro 15, 18, 11. Humans: RAVEN 84.67 percent; IntelligenceTest 30 to 93.4 percent per question vs best model 18 percent.
limits: GPT-4V and Gemini Pro era (early 2024). Exact column order of the random row is read from a garbled table.
agent_relevance: Perception, not strategy, is the first bottleneck for image matrices. Do not read strategy effects without controlling perception.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) How Far Are We, section 5: three-stage diagnosis
finding: Split the task into perception, rule deduction, and hypothesis verification. Perception is the worst stage (compounding and confounding description errors). Giving oracle text descriptions helps a lot. Adding an oracle rationale (the rule in words, no answer) on top did NOT help much.
numbers: Text-only in-context example: 100 percent. Image plus text: 80 percent. Image only query: 20 percent. Oracle description plus oracle rationale: no significant gain over oracle description alone (3 hand-made RPMs, 10 repeats each). Segmenting the image into 9 question cells and 6 options reduced description errors.
limits: Only three hand-built RPMs for the stage analysis, so tiny N.
agent_relevance: Even when the rule is known, turning it into the right answer is a separate failure (the build step). Check the produced cell, not only the stated rule (G3, G10).

source: Zhang et al. (2024) How Far Are We, section 5.3: strategy observation
finding: Direct observation of strategy: strong models such as GPT-4V often use the answer options together with the grid to form and test hypotheses, rather than generating a hypothesis from the grid alone and then checking for a match. This is the response-elimination / option-informed style.
numbers: Qualitative, from reasoning traces on 3 hand-made RPMs. No frequency reported.
quote: they often use the answer options along with the grid to form and tests hypotheses
limits: Anecdote, not a coded sample. Possibly an artifact of prompt format that lists options.
agent_relevance: Default LLM behaviour with options visible leans toward elimination. To force construction, hide the options until after a built answer exists.

source: Cao et al. (2024/25) What is the Visual Cognition Gap between Humans and Multimodal LLMs? (VCog-Bench, MaRs-VQA), vision vs language bottleneck
finding: When the options are removed (question image only), models are at chance: they cannot build the answer from the matrix alone. Adding option images lifts accuracy a lot, especially for a fine-tuned model. Adding perfect text descriptions helps only a little. The authors read this as shallow pattern matching against options.
numbers: MaRs-VQA (4 options, chance 25): GPT-4o 24.58 percent question only; 33.96 with options; 36.46 with options plus oracle descriptions. Qwen2-VCog (fine-tuned): 26.32, 72.71, 71.43. Human adults 81 percent (N=659 across ages 11 to 33 in the source study).
quote: both GPT-4o and Qwen2-VCog perform at near chance level when deprived of option images
limits: 4-option task. Question-only condition is a pure construction test but no construction output was scored for similarity.
agent_relevance: Evidence that current vision models lean on response elimination (matching options) and cannot construct. For text-only agent matrices, the construct-first path may be stronger than for vision models.

source: Cao et al. (2025) VCog-Bench, multi-round option-elimination prompting
finding: An LLM-agent-style loop that uses explicit response elimination: step-by-step option elimination, then the model reflects on its answer and reruns the reasoning if it judges the answer wrong. It beats single-pass chain of thought but is slower, and does not close the gap to o1 or humans.
numbers: GPT-4o on MaRs-VQA: CoT 33.96 percent; CoT 1-shot 35.22; 3-shot 36.10; 5-shot 36.03; multi-round elimination CoT 41.96; plus 1-shot 42.08. GPT-o1 52.29. Human adult 81.00.
limits: Same-benchmark single study. Self-reflection used the model's own correctness judgement; no ablation separating elimination from reflection.
agent_relevance: Elimination plus retry gives about +8 points on a weak vision model. Evidence for keeping elimination as a fallback check, not as the first move. Note the confound: it also re-asks after a self-judged wrong answer (a doubt loop; G1 says doubt only on a signal).

source: Cao et al. (2025) VCog-Bench, fine-tuning on reasoning chains
finding: Fine-tuning Qwen2-VL on matrix items with reasoning annotations reaches near human accuracy in distribution, but barely transfers to RAVEN. Without the reasoning strings, accuracy drops about 18 points. This hints at shortcut learning.
numbers: Qwen2-VCog with reasoning: MaRs-VQA 72.71, RAVEN 31.96. Without reasoning strings: 54.82 and 29.30. Base Qwen2-VL on RAVEN: 15.36 zero-shot (chance 12.5). Authors' raw note: RAVEN rose from 29.27 to 31.96.
limits: Training set is not the scaffold route; relevant only as an upper bound on what pattern matching buys.
agent_relevance: Reasoning traces matter for in-distribution gains but do not guarantee transfer; do not trust a strategy that wins on one matrix family.

source: Ahrabian et al. (2024) The Curious Case of Nonverbal Abstract Reasoning with Multi-Modal LLMs
finding: Across open and closed MLLMs on RPM-style sets (IQ50, RAVEN-S, CCSE), the best accuracy is within about 2 percent of the majority baseline, so numbers may reflect output bias (always answering one option). Scaling with model size did not hold. Models were descriptive, not logical, in their reasoning.
numbers: Best model accuracy is within about 2 percent of the majority baseline. Models land within [-8.7, +7.3] percent of random on the first dataset. Zero-shot per-model cells for IQ50 and RAVEN-S are partly garbled in the extracted table (for example llava-1.5-13b 0.480 in one column, gpt-4v 0.26 in another), so no per-model figure is used.
limits: Column assignment in the extracted table is partly garbled. Early 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Check for option-position bias when scoring option-based answers. Majority-baseline equality is a warning sign of elimination by habit.

source: Ahrabian et al. (2024), guided prompting on IQ50
finding: Giving a general hint or a sample-specific hint hurt GPT-4V and Gemini. An interactive corrective hint (fix the most prominent error in the model's own reasoning) helped a lot. In-context demonstrations from a different dataset did not help much.
numbers: Corrective hints improved performance by as much as 100 percent (relative) for gpt-4v on IQ50; general and sample-specific hints reduced accuracy. 5-shot symmetric ICL, 5 seeds, in-distribution vs out-of-distribution (RAVEN-S) demos tested.
limits: Small IQ50 set (50 items). Relative gains from a low base.
agent_relevance: Targeted correction after a failed check works; blanket strategy instructions can hurt. Matches G1: act on a signal, not by schedule.

source: Gendron et al. (2023/24) Large Language Models Are Not Strong Abstract Reasoners
finding: Text RAVEN (RAVEN-T) compared open-ended vs multiple-choice. Giving options helps all models systematically, but accuracy stays low. Models cannot recognise the right answer even when it is shown. The authors conclude LLMs are poor evaluators on abstract reasoning tasks.
numbers: GPT-4 on RAVEN-T: open-ended 0.410 (text) and 0.330 (symbolic); multiple-choice 0.697 (text) and 0.535 (symbolic); chance 0.125. GPT-3.5-Turbo MC 0.315 text, 0.276 symbolic. Text-Davinci-3 MC 0.452 and 0.461 vs open 0.343 and 0.234.
quote: the models cannot recognise the proper solution among the other choices
limits: Different datasets, mixed model families. MC and open are not matched by a build-then-compare pipeline: the open answer is scored by exact match, not by choosing the nearest option.
agent_relevance: Shows what options add: a +17 to +29 point lift for GPT-4. That lift is what a build-then-match pipeline must keep; the open answer alone is weaker.

source: Gendron et al. (2023/24), chain-of-thought and refinement
finding: Chain-of-thought did not improve RAVEN-T results overall. It helped on some datasets for GPT-4 and hurt on others. Self-refinement strategies also did not fix abstract reasoning. Fine-tuning a small model reaches near-perfect in distribution but only partly transfers.
numbers: CoT, RAVEN-T open: GPT-4-cot 0.385 text and 0.354 symbolic (vs 0.410 and 0.330 plain); GPT-3.5-Turbo-cot 0.302 and 0.211 (vs 0.226 and 0.161). CoT MC: GPT-4-cot 0.596 text, 0.517 symbolic (vs 0.697 and 0.535 plain); GPT-3.5-cot 0.257 and 0.144.
limits: 2023 model versions, 128 or 512 token limits. Not a reasoning-model test.
agent_relevance: Longer thinking is not a cure here (consistent with G11). A check should be an external check, not the model's own judging.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: On a text matrix task (Digit Matrices, rule structure like Raven's SPM) GPT-3 beat human undergraduates in both generative and multiple-choice formats. The multiple-choice advantage was larger. Rule-type difficulty profile resembled humans (progression harder, spatial permutation harder).
numbers: Generative accuracy: GPT-3 vs 40 UCLA students, odds ratio 1.88 (p = 0.005, CI 1.21 to 2.91). Multiple choice: odds ratio 6.27 (p = 2.3e-8, CI 3.28 to 11.99). Correlation of difficulty across 32 subtypes r(30) = 0.39 (p = 0.027). Humans ran a free-response answer first, then the choice.
limits: Zero-shot, digits not images. Choice scored by mean token log-probability of each completed option, a likelihood ranking (elimination-like). 3 participants excluded for random answers; 40 kept in experiment 1.
agent_relevance: Humans in this study did generate-then-choose; GPT-3 scoring was choice-only. The gap between formats suggests the choice step is where models gain easily.

source: Hu, Storks, Lewis, Chai (2023) In-Context Analogical Reasoning with Pre-Trained Language Models
finding: Language models on visual RAVEN converted to text. Each candidate completed matrix is scored by the model, so this is response elimination by likelihood. Abstractions (naming attributes, splitting by attribute) raise accuracy a lot. Models are above chance even when given no complete rows, which points to answer-set priors.
numbers: GPT-3 175B accuracy by rows shown (1 row / 2 rows / 3 rows incl. human): Center 36.8, 69.2, 77.2 vs human 95.6; 2x2 grid 54.0, 71.0, 78.0 vs 81.8; 3x3 grid 73.0, 85.2, 86.4 vs 79.6. Chance 12.5. Some small models double from 22.2 to 45.6 with abstraction.
limits: Original RAVEN has the central-candidate shortcut (see c20); the authors checked a subset on I-RAVEN and found comparable results. Third-row-only result is above chance, a sign of shortcuts or priors.
agent_relevance: Option-scoring alone reaches human-level on easy configurations. It is a strong baseline that construct-first must beat. Always run a no-context control (c20).

source: Zhang, Gao, Jia, Zhu, Zhu (2019) RAVEN: A Dataset for Relational and Analogical Visual rEasoNing
finding: The dataset behind most RPM-model tests. Human accuracy on the RAVEN set is 84.41 percent overall. The answer set was built by changing one attribute of the correct panel at a time, which gives a bias that models can exploit.
numbers: Human overall 84.41 percent; sub-configuration human accuracies 79.55 to 95.45 percent (human row of results table).
limits: Only the human table and generation section were read, not all models. Answer-set design is the issue in c20.
agent_relevance: Any LLM result on original RAVEN that works from options alone can be an elimination shortcut, not reasoning.

source: Hu, Zhang, Wang, et al. (2021 AAAI; arXiv 2020) Stratified Rule-Aware Network for Abstract Visual Reasoning (introduces I-RAVEN)
finding: In original RAVEN the correct answer can be found without looking at the context matrix: pick the candidate that shares the most attribute values with the others (the central node of the candidate graph). Models trained on candidates only match or beat models that see the context. The fix is I-RAVEN, where distractors are generated by balanced attribute bisection, so a context-blind model is at chance.
numbers: Table 1: ResNet 53.4 percent on RAVEN vs context-blind ResNet 71.9; CoPINet 91.4 vs context-blind CoPINet 94.2. On I-RAVEN context-blind models drop to about 12.5 percent (random). SRAN scores 60.8 on I-RAVEN and 60.7 on RAVEN.
quote: the correct answer can be found when only presented with the answer set
limits: Neural models, not LLMs. The shortcut is a pure response-elimination heuristic (most-similar-to-others).
agent_relevance: Gold-standard control: run option-only and context-only prompts. If option-only scores above chance, the item set rewards elimination.

source: Yang, McGreggor, Kunda (2022) Visual-Imagery-Based Analogical Construction in Geometric Matrix Reasoning Task
finding: A non-LLM imagery-based model (ASTI, ASTI+) is built to follow constructive matching strictly (ASTI) or option-informed construction (ASTI+, uses options to tune alignment parameters). Strategies that maximise only option-match (O) are far weaker than strategies that weigh the quality of the constructed explanation (MAT) as the matrix grows to 3x3.
numbers: Standard RPM (60 items): M-neutral and M-prudent solve 57/60; M-confident 55/60; O-only strategies much lower, especially on the 3x3 sets C, D, E (A and B are 2x2). Model range overlaps human percentiles.
quote: high-achieving test takers usually take a more constructive approach
limits: Hand-built representations on one test; not LLMs. Distractors in RPM are designed as traps for strategies that only maximise option match.
agent_relevance: Computational support that score = explanation quality plus option fit beats option fit alone, on 3x3 items. Relevant to S4: test both the rule fit and the candidate fit.

source: Yang, McGreggor, Kunda (2022), strategy taxonomy
finding: Defines three options-use patterns formally. Constructive matching: infer T, apply T to build A, test A. Response elimination: infer T1 from the matrix, infer T2 using option O, compare, eliminate O if they fail. Option-informed construction sits between. Notes that human strategy choice relates to ability, item type and difficulty.
numbers: No numbers (definition section citing Snow 1981 and Bethell-Fox et al. 1984).
limits: Formal definition, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Gives the exact definitions to specify S3 (build from examples) versus a fallback elimination test in S4.

source: Yang, McGreggor, Kunda line cited in Modeling Gestalt Visual Reasoning on RPM Using Generative Image Inpainting (2019)
finding: Review remark in a generative-inpainting RPM paper: knowledge-based RPM models come in both strategies (Carpenter et al. 1990 matched relations with five rules; others), but ALL the data-driven (neural) models follow response elimination. The authors' own generative inpainting model uses constructive matching without deliberate reasoning.
numbers: No accuracy needed for this line; paper gives the categorisation only.
quote: all of the data-driven models follow the response-elimination approach
limits: One author team's classification, from 2019.
agent_relevance: Historical base rate: trained AI systems default to elimination. An LLM scaffold that forces construction is a departure from the default.

source: Jiang et al. (2024) MARVEL: Multidimensional Abstraction and Reasoning through Visual Evaluation and Learning
finding: On a new abstract puzzle set with six patterns, all nine multimodal models are near random while humans reach 68.86 percent. Few-shot CoT does not help. Perception questions show models cannot see the details. With accurate text descriptions added, a subset jumps and GPT-4V reaches human level.
numbers: Human 68.86 percent (SD 9.74; 30 annotators aged 10 to 50). Closed-source models average 25.7 percent, open-source 24.0 percent; gap about 40 points. Best group accuracy with consistent perception and reasoning 5.97 percent. With text descriptions on a subset: 11.57 percent to 44.21 percent; GPT-4V 65.26 percent. Some models pick one option index nearly always (BLIP2 always choice 1; Claude 3 Sonnet and Gemini mostly choice 4).
limits: Not classical RPM, but option-based abstract puzzles. Small human sample.
agent_relevance: Option-index bias is a measured sign of habitual elimination. Perception and strategy must be separated before drawing strategy conclusions.

source: Li (2025) A Study of Rule Omission in Raven's Progressive Matrices
finding: A sequence-to-sequence transformer that GENERATES the missing panel token by token (a constructive format) is strong on rules seen in training and falls sharply on omitted rules. High token-level accuracy hides low whole-answer accuracy because candidate answers differ by one attribute token.
numbers: One-rule-omitted token accuracy up to 96.88 percent (Center) but full-answer accuracy only 45.31 percent. Average accuracy drops from 47.00 to 31.47 percent when removing two rules instead of one (Different-rule condition) and stays 92.62 to 93.42 percent when test rules were seen.
limits: Trained small models on I-RAVEN, not prompted LLMs. Generative format.
agent_relevance: One slip in a constructed answer flips the final pick. A build step needs exact comparison to the candidates plus a check, not a close-enough match.

source: NeuroCognition authors (2026) A Neuropsychologically Grounded Evaluation of LLM Cognitive Abilities
finding: Models were given the same Raven items with options (multiple choice) and without (generate). The format effect has no single direction: some models gain from options, others lose. The authors link MC to quick elimination and generation to building an answer from internal rules. Models do better on text than images, while humans show the opposite.
numbers: RAPM text, MC then generative: GPT-5 0.540 to 0.605; Claude 0.560 to 0.385; Grok 4 Fast 0.690 to 0.555. Humans: image 0.814 (from RAVEN paper); text pilot 0.430 (MC) and 0.444 (generative), N=9 each. Chance 1/8. Image set 140 items (20 per configuration); text set 200 items.
quote: MC gives a small set of choices and rewards quick elimination in trade of distraction
limits: Single run per cell as reported; item counts small; Claude's drop is large and unexplained. Explanation about elimination is the authors' reading, not tested with a strategy probe.
agent_relevance: Newest data (2026): constructing is not uniformly better for current frontier models. Whether to hide options should be a per-class measured choice, not a fixed rule.

source: Mitchell, Palmarini, Moskvichev (2023) Comparing Humans, GPT-4, and GPT-4V on Abstraction and Reasoning Tasks
finding: On ConceptARC, a generate-the-output-grid task with no answer options, text GPT-4 is far below humans. GPT-4V on the 48 simplest tasks is also far below, and a one-shot visual prompt did not help. No options means the model has to construct the answer.
numbers: Humans 91 percent overall; first-place Kaggle ARC program 52 percent; GPT-4 25 percent on ConceptARC text (with simple zero-shot prompt). GPT-4V on 48 minimal tasks: 0.23 one-shot, 0.25 zero-shot.
limits: Not Raven-style; included as the no-options pure construction case. 2023 models; reasoning models since then score far higher on ARC.
agent_relevance: For pure construction tasks (no option set), one-shot prompts alone were not enough. Needs a check step (S4) on the built output.
